title: How to read your Black Friday numbers like for like
summary: This year's Black Friday comparison is easy to get wrong. Compare the right numbers on the right days, then read what sold out, what shoppers couldn't find and which first rows earned their place.
body_markdown:
The week after Cyber Monday, someone will open the numbers and ask whether the weekend beat last year. It's a fair question, and this year it's easy to answer wrong. Three things changed that have nothing to do with how your sale went. Shopify counts visits differently, Black Friday moved a day, and your search report may not be counting what you think.


Here is how to compare the weekend fairly, the three reads worth an afternoon once it's over, and the one question the weekend can't answer. Set up the comparison before Black Friday and the answer is ready when someone asks.


## Shopify counts sessions differently this year


In September, Shopify changed how its analytics counts sessions. Bots are now filtered out by default, a session no longer ends at midnight, and some visits that go straight to checkout count where they didn't before. Shopify says sessions can come out higher or lower because of it, and[its own help page](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/reports-and-analytics/discrepancies/session-measurement-update) tells merchants to treat the change as a new starting line. On November 16 it[improved its bot detection](https://changelog.shopify.com/posts/improved-bot-detection-for-cart-and-checkout-activity) again.


So this year's sessions in Shopify's reports aren't counted the way last year's were, and neither is anything worked out from them. Shopify itself points out that conversion rate can move when orders haven't, simply because the sessions underneath it changed.


Orders and sales were left out of both changes. Lead with those:


- Orders
- Net sales
- Units sold
- Average order value


Keep sessions and conversion rate for comparing days within this year's sale, where both sides are counted the same way. And treat net sales from the week after as a first read, since the weekend's returns will keep arriving for weeks. If bots have troubled your numbers all year, our[guide to Shopify bot traffic](https://depict.ai/resources/guides/shopify-bot-traffic) covers what to filter.


## Count from Black Friday, not from the date


Black Friday was November 28 last year and November 27 this year. Line up this year's weekend with the same dates last year and your Black Friday sits against last year's Thanksgiving.


Compare the same days counted from Black Friday instead, this year's Friday to Monday against last year's, which ended on December 1. Shopify's reports have a Black Friday Cyber Monday preset for both the dates and the comparison. If you set the dates by hand, count from the Friday.


If your sale runs all week, compare the whole week as well as the weekend. In Sweden,[Statistics Sweden](https://www.scb.se/pressmeddelande/hushall-handlar-for-flera-miljarder-mer-under-black-week/) found that household spending rises across the whole of Black Week, most clearly on the Friday (November 2025). Do it market by market, since the weekend weighs differently in each.


## Is your search report counting every search?


Shopify's own search reports count searches that reach its search results page. They leave out the suggestions that drop down as a shopper types, so a shopper who taps a suggested product never shows up. If a search app, or a search that opens over the page, has replaced Shopify's, its numbers live in that tool's own report. And if you switched search this year, the two halves of the year were counted by different tools, so compare what shoppers searched for rather than how many searches there were.


## Three reads worth an afternoon


Once the comparison is fair, put the weekend to work. These three tell you what to reorder, what to fix and what to keep. Shopify's search and sell-through reports can run up to three days behind, so give them until the Thursday after Cyber Monday to take in the whole weekend.


### What sold out, and in which sizes


A product that sold out at full price, or on a light discount, is the clearest signal you get all year. It tells you what to reorder if you can and what to buy deeper next year. A product that only sold out at 40% off tells you about the discount. Look at the sizes too, because the sizes that went first show where your depth was wrong.


Shopify's **Total sales by product variant** report shows the weekend size by size, and **Products by sell-through rate** shows how much of each variant's stock went. Read sell-through for this year only, since Shopify changed the stock figure behind it on October 1. Our[post on sell-through rate](https://depict.ai/resources/blog/how-to-use-sell-through-rate) covers how to use it before you mark anything down.


### What shoppers searched for and didn't find


A search with no results is a shopper telling you what they wanted. Shopify's **Searches with no results** report lists them. Some are products you don't sell yet. Others are products you do sell under a different word, because they typed "jumper" and your catalog says sweater. Sort the list into three piles, things to buy, things to rename and words to add. Read it as a list of words rather than a count against last year, since the September change touched search counts too. Our post on[testing your site search like a shopper](https://depict.ai/resources/blog/test-site-search-like-a-shopper) shows how to fix the last two piles.


### Whether your first rows earned their place


You probably pinned products to the top of your sale collections. A sales report tells you what each one sold, but not where it sat or how many shoppers scrolled past it. That's the part worth knowing. A pin that everyone saw and few bought took a spot a better product could have used. A pin that's there to tell the story of a drop has a different job, so judge it on that.


This is the read Depict is built for. Open a collection's performance view and you see each product's position and its average position over the period, how many shoppers saw it in the grid and how many clicked, and which pins earned their place. Clicks, orders, sell-through and revenue can sit on every product card while you arrange the collection, so the next sale starts from what this one taught you.


## The question the weekend can't answer


Did my change cause this? A peak lifts everything at once. A bigger campaign or a better email raises every page, so a collection that beat last year may simply have ridden the tide, and the weekend can't tell you whether your new sort order, your pins or your new search made the difference.


Ask it after the January sale, on one collection that sells steadily. Split shoppers between two versions of it for two or three weeks, say one with your pins and one without, and compare what each sold. On Shopify, Depict runs that test for you and tells you in plain words which version did better, or that there's no clear difference yet.


Write the three reads down the week after, while the weekend is fresh. They are next season's plan, and our seasonal guide on[ending a season on purpose](https://depict.ai/resources/guides/seasonal-merchandising#wind-down) has the rest.
